author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary pressure demands.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow and identify which structures each valve separates.

modules.description: Two paired heart models introduce anatomical orientation, patient right/left, apex position, and the relationship between exterior great vessels and internal chambers.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the human heart anatomically with apex inferior and slightly leftward.
Compare an intact exterior heart with an anterior cutaway heart.
Explain why patient right and left appear reversed to the viewer.
instructions: Place the models on a tabletop-sized surface about arm's length away.
Advance through the clips to compare the intact and cutaway hearts.
Use the labels to keep patient orientation separate from viewer orientation.

components.text: Exterior and Cutaway Heart Orientation
Patient RIGHT is on your left; patient LEFT is on your right.

clips.changeMeaning: The paired intact and cutaway heart models are presented side by side to establish exterior-to-interior comparison throughout the lab.
clips.narration: The lab opens with two coordinated views. The intact heart on the left shows the exterior surface and great vessels. The cutaway heart on the right has the anterior wall removed so the chambers, septum, and valves can be examined.

components.text: Apex inferior-left; great vessels at the base

clips.changeMeaning: An apex arrow appears and the cutaway model tilts slightly to help students anchor the gross three-dimensional orientation of the heart.
clips.narration: The apex points inferiorly and slightly toward the patient's left. The base is the superior region where the aorta, pulmonary trunk, venae cavae, and pulmonary veins attach.

clips.changeMeaning: A right-left orientation label appears to prevent the common error of naming structures from the viewer's perspective.
clips.narration: Anatomical right and left are named from the patient's perspective. When you face the heart, the patient's right side appears on your left, and the patient's left side appears on your right.

components.text: Great vessels enter and leave near the base

clips.changeMeaning: The intact heart enlarges slightly while the cutaway heart reduces slightly, shifting attention to surface vessels before the structural tour.
clips.narration: On the exterior model, notice the major vessels entering and leaving near the base: superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary trunk and arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta. These will be identified in detail next.

modules.description: A sequential tour highlights the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels, with matching labels for interior and exterior landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four heart chambers in anatomical position.
Identify the tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, and aortic valves and state what each separates.
Identify the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta.
instructions: Follow the yellow highlight and read the structure label.
Compare the highlighted internal region with the exterior model beside it.
Pay attention to the dual name mitral/bicuspid valve.

components.text: Structure label
Structural Tour: Chambers → Valves → Vessels

Right atrium
Receives SVC and IVC blood

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight identifies the right atrium and connects it to the corresponding exterior region receiving systemic venous blood.
clips.narration: First locate the right atrium. It receives deoxygenated blood from the superior and inferior vena cava. In the anterior cutaway, remember that patient right is on your left.

components.text:
Right ventricle
Pumps to pulmonary circuit

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves inferiorly to the right ventricle, linking chamber position to pulmonary outflow function.
clips.narration: Below the right atrium is the right ventricle. It pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

components.text:
Left atrium and left ventricle
Receive from lungs; pump to body

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight shifts to the left-sided chambers and changes red, separating oxygenated left-heart flow from the blue right-heart flow.
clips.narration: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins. The left ventricle below it pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and systemic circulation.

components.text:
Valves
Tricuspid: RA→RV
Pulmonary: RV→pulmonary trunk
Mitral/bicuspid: LA→LV
Aortic: LV→aorta

clips.changeMeaning: A compact highlight at the valve plane emphasizes the four named valves and the boundaries they guard.
clips.narration: The four valves are the tricuspid valve between right atrium and right ventricle, pulmonary valve between right ventricle and pulmonary trunk, mitral or bicuspid valve between left atrium and left ventricle, and aortic valve between left ventricle and aorta.

components.text:
Great vessels
SVC, IVC, pulmonary arteries,
pulmonary veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight expands over the base of both heart models to consolidate the great vessels after students have located chambers and valves.
clips.narration: The major vessels are the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward the heart.

modules.description: Animated blue and red flow paths show steady-state circulation and distinguish the pulmonary loop from the systemic loop.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Use blue and red color coding to distinguish deoxygenated and oxygenated blood.
Explain the right heart's role in pulmonary circulation and the left heart's role in systemic circulation.
Correctly interpret pulmonary arteries and veins by flow direction rather than oxygen content.
instructions: Watch the blue and red streams fill the cutaway heart and vessels.
Observe the pulmonary loop highlight, then the systemic loop highlight.
Use the color key to explain what each side of the heart is pumping.

components.text: Blue = deoxygenated   |   Red = oxygenated
Color key: blue deoxygenated, red oxygenated

clips.changeMeaning: Both flow paths are shown with a color key so students can interpret oxygenation state before the circuits are separated.
clips.narration: Blue represents deoxygenated blood and red represents oxygenated blood. In the heart, the right side carries blue blood and the left side carries red blood.

components.text: Pulmonary circuit: right heart → lungs → left heart

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary loop ribbon appears to isolate the right-heart-to-lungs circuit and show its return to the left atrium.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circuit runs from the right heart to the lungs and back to the left heart. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into pulmonary arteries, and pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood.

components.text: Systemic circuit: left heart → body → right heart

clips.changeMeaning: The systemic loop ribbon replaces the pulmonary highlight to contrast the body circuit with the lung circuit.
clips.narration: The systemic circuit runs from the left heart to the body and back to the right heart. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for distribution to body tissues.

components.text: Artery = away from heart   |   Vein = toward heart

clips.changeMeaning: Both loop ribbons appear faintly together while the label states the artery-versus-vein naming rule used in both circuits.
clips.narration: Pulmonary arteries and veins can be confusing. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood toward the heart, regardless of oxygen content.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single enlarged red blood cell advances through the full circuit, changing from blue to red in lung capillaries and back to blue after systemic exchange.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace a blood cell through the full circulatory sequence in order.
Name each chamber, valve, and vessel as the cell enters it.
Identify lung capillaries as the site of oxygen pickup and systemic capillaries as the site of oxygen delivery.
instructions: Press Next to move the cell to the next structure.
Read the label aloud before advancing to practice the sequence.
Replay this scene until you can trace the pathway without prompts.

components.text: Start: Superior vena cava
Superior vena cava → Right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blue cell starts in the superior vena cava region and the label identifies the first chamber entered, the right atrium.
clips.narration: Begin in the superior vena cava. Deoxygenated blood from the upper body enters the right atrium.

components.text: Tricuspid valve → Right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The cell moves downward through the tricuspid valve plane into the right ventricle, marking the first valve crossing.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

components.text: Pulmonary valve → Pulmonary trunk/arteries

clips.changeMeaning: The cell moves toward the pulmonary outflow tract and the label emphasizes that pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, pushing the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries. These arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the heart.

components.text: Lung capillaries: oxygen pickup

clips.changeMeaning: The lung capillary bed appears and the blood cell changes color at the gas exchange site.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, the cell releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. The cell changes from blue to red to show oxygenation.

components.text: Pulmonary veins → Left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The red cell returns from the lung capillary bed to the left atrium through pulmonary veins, reinforcing vessel naming by direction.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins and enters the left atrium. These are veins because they return blood toward the heart.

components.text: Mitral/bicuspid valve → Left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The cell moves into the left ventricle and the label uses both mitral and bicuspid valve names.
clips.narration: The left atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, into the left ventricle.

components.text: Aortic valve → Aorta → Systemic arteries

clips.changeMeaning: The red cell advances into the aortic outflow and toward the body capillary bed, showing systemic ejection.
clips.narration: The left ventricle contracts forcefully, pushing the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and then through systemic arteries to body tissues.

components.text:
Systemic veins → Superior vena cava
Loop complete

clips.changeMeaning: The cell changes back to blue and returns to the starting superior vena cava position to close the complete circuit.
clips.narration: In systemic capillaries, oxygen is delivered to tissues. The cell becomes deoxygenated again and returns through systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the loop.

modules.description: Side-by-side ventricular cross-sections compare the thin right ventricular myocardium with the thick left ventricular myocardium and relate thickness to pressure demands.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare myocardial wall thickness in right and left ventricles.
State typical healthy adult ranges: right ventricle about 3–5 mm and left ventricle about 10–15 mm.
Relate thicker left ventricular myocardium to the higher pressure needed for systemic circulation.
instructions: Compare the cross-sections at the same scale.
Use the caliper markers to estimate the relative thickness difference.
Connect the structural difference to pulmonary versus systemic resistance.

components.text: Ventricular Wall Thickness
Same-level cross-sections through the ventricles

clips.changeMeaning: Two ventricular cross-sections appear at the same scale to support direct comparison of myocardial thickness.
clips.narration: These cross-sections are cut at the same horizontal level through the ventricles. The right ventricle is shown on the left, and the left ventricle is shown on the right.

components.text: Right ventricle: thin wall, about 3–5 mm

clips.changeMeaning: The right ventricular wall highlight and small caliper appear to associate thin myocardium with low pulmonary pressure.
clips.narration: The right ventricular myocardium is relatively thin, often about three to five millimeters in a healthy adult. It pumps only to the nearby lungs, a low-pressure circuit.

components.text: Left ventricle: thick wall, about 10–15 mm

clips.changeMeaning: The highlight moves to the left ventricular wall and the larger caliper emphasizes the greater thickness and pressure requirement.
clips.narration: The left ventricular myocardium is much thicker, often about ten to fifteen millimeters. It must generate enough pressure to perfuse the entire systemic circuit.

components.text: LV wall ≈ 3× RV wall: systemic circuit requires higher pressure

clips.changeMeaning: Both highlights and calipers appear together so students can visually confirm the approximate three-to-one thickness ratio.
clips.narration: The left ventricular wall is roughly three times thicker than the right ventricular wall. This is a form-function relationship: more resistance in the systemic circuit requires more muscular force.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: Open and closed valve models demonstrate atrioventricular versus semilunar valve behavior during ventricular relaxation and contraction.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Classify tricuspid and mitral valves as atrioventricular valves.
Classify pulmonary and aortic valves as semilunar valves.
Explain which valve set is open or closed during ventricular filling and ventricular contraction.
Describe how valves prevent backflow through pressure-driven closure.
instructions: Step through the valve states and compare open versus closed models.
Notice which valves protect the atria and which protect the ventricles.
Use the phase labels to distinguish ventricular relaxation from ventricular contraction.

components.text: Valve Function: Preventing Backflow
AV valves: tricuspid, mitral | Semilunar: pulmonary, aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The valve plane is highlighted and all four valve positions are labeled conceptually as AV or semilunar.
clips.narration: The atrioventricular valves are the tricuspid and mitral valves between atria and ventricles. The semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves between ventricles and outflow arteries.

components.text: Ventricular relaxation: AV open, semilunar closed

clips.changeMeaning: The valve prefabs represent relaxation: AV valves are open and semilunar valves are closed, matching ventricular filling.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation and filling, the atrioventricular valves are open so blood can enter the ventricles. The semilunar valves are closed to stop arterial blood from returning to the ventricles.

components.text: Ventricular contraction: AV closed, semilunar open

clips.changeMeaning: The valve prefabs swap to represent contraction: AV valves are closed and semilunar valves are open, matching ventricular ejection.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, ventricular pressure closes the atrioventricular valves to prevent backflow into the atria. The pulmonary and aortic valves open for ejection into arteries.

components.text: Pressure-driven closure: forward flow allowed, backflow blocked

clips.changeMeaning: A broad highlight covers all valve positions while the label summarizes pressure-driven closure and backflow prevention.
clips.narration: Valves open and close because of pressure differences. Their job is to allow forward flow and block reverse flow: AV valves protect the atria, and semilunar valves protect the ventricles.

modules.description: An unlabeled cutaway heart highlights structures and presents candidate names for students to identify chambers, valves, and vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify unlabeled chambers, valves, and great vessels from highlighted regions.
Differentiate similar structures such as pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins.
Reinforce patient right-left orientation while naming structures.
instructions: Read the highlighted prompt and choose the best candidate name.
Advance to reveal feedback, then continue to the next highlighted structure.
Replay this module for additional identification practice.

components.text: Identify the highlighted structure.

A. Right atrium
B. Left atrium
C. Aorta
D. Mitral valve
Feedback appears here.

A. Right atrium
B. Left atrium
C. Aorta
D. Mitral valve

clips.changeMeaning: The right atrium is highlighted without a direct label, and plausible choices are displayed for student identification.
clips.narration: Quiz prompt one. Identify the highlighted chamber. It receives blood from the superior and inferior vena cava.

components.text: Correct: Right atrium — receives systemic venous blood.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms the chamber and connects it to its inflow vessels and outflow valve.
clips.narration: Correct answer: right atrium. It receives systemic venous blood and sends it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

components.text:
A. Pulmonary valve
B. Tricuspid valve
C. Aortic valve
D. Pulmonary vein

clips.changeMeaning: The aortic valve region is highlighted, requiring students to connect a valve to its chamber-vessel boundary.
clips.narration: Quiz prompt two. Identify the highlighted valve. It lies between the left ventricle and the aorta.

components.text: Correct: Aortic valve — between LV and aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms the aortic valve and reinforces its role in preventing backflow into the left ventricle.
clips.narration: Correct answer: aortic valve. This semilunar valve opens during left ventricular ejection and closes to prevent backflow from the aorta.

components.text:
A. Pulmonary arteries
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Superior vena cava
D. Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The pulmonary vein entry region is highlighted to test a common confusion between pulmonary veins and pulmonary arteries.
clips.narration: Quiz prompt three. Identify the highlighted vessels. They return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium.

components.text: Correct: Pulmonary veins — toward heart and oxygenated.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback clarifies that pulmonary veins are named by direction toward the heart, not oxygen content.
clips.narration: Correct answer: pulmonary veins. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, even though they carry oxygenated blood.

modules.moduleName: Scene 8: Blood Flow Tracing Quiz and Recap
modules.description: A flow-sequence quiz asks students to select the next structure in circulation, followed by a summary of the lab's five main concept areas.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict the next structure in the heart-lung-body blood flow pathway.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins in sequence context.
Summarize structural anatomy, dual circulation, RBC path, wall thickness asymmetry, and valve function.
instructions: For each prompt, choose the next structure in the pathway.
Use direction, color, and chamber position as clues.
Review the recap board and replay any scene that remains unclear.

components.text: Blood has just entered the right atrium. What is next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium
Recap
Blood in right atrium: what comes next?

A. Tricuspid valve
B. Pulmonary veins
C. Aortic valve
D. Left atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The cell is placed in the right atrium and the choices test the first valve crossing in the flow pathway.
clips.narration: Flow quiz one: a unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. The next structure is the tricuspid valve, which leads to the right ventricle.

components.text: Blood in pulmonary arteries: what comes next?

A. Lung capillaries
B. Left ventricle
C. Pulmonary veins
D. Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The cell relocates to the pulmonary arteries and the choices emphasize that the next destination is the lungs, not the left heart directly.
clips.narration: Flow quiz two: blood in the pulmonary arteries goes next to the lung capillaries, where gas exchange oxygenates the blood.

components.text: Blood in left ventricle: what valve is next?

A. Aortic valve
B. Mitral valve
C. Pulmonary valve
D. Inferior vena cava

clips.changeMeaning: The cell becomes red in the left ventricle and the choices target the systemic outflow valve.
clips.narration: Flow quiz three: oxygenated blood in the left ventricle leaves through the aortic valve and enters the aorta for systemic circulation.

components.text:
1. Structural inventory
Chambers: RA, RV, LA, LV
Valves: tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral/bicuspid, aortic
Vessels: SVC, IVC, pulmonary arteries/veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The quiz heart and cell are hidden and a summary board appears with the structural inventory highlighted as the first recap item.
clips.narration: Recap concept one: structural inventory. You identified the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels entering and leaving the heart.

components.text:
2. Dual circulation
Pulmonary: right heart → lungs → left heart
Systemic: left heart → body → right heart
Blue = deoxygenated; red = oxygenated

clips.changeMeaning: The recap board updates to summarize pulmonary and systemic circuit organization and oxygenation color coding.
clips.narration: Recap concept two: dual circulation. The right heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the left heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body.

components.text:
3. Blood path
SVC/IVC → RA → tricuspid → RV → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → mitral → LV → aortic valve → aorta

4. Wall thickness
LV myocardium ≈ 3× RV: higher systemic pressure

5. Valves prevent backflow
Relaxation: AV open, semilunar closed
Contraction: AV closed, semilunar open

clips.changeMeaning: The final board consolidates the blood path, ventricular wall thickness asymmetry, and valve state patterns into a compact study checklist.
clips.narration: Final recap: trace the full blood path in order, explain why the left ventricle is thicker, and describe valves as pressure-driven structures that prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.
